title: This Copier Company Once Had a Shot at Being Bigger Than Apple and Microsoft Combined
excerpt: "If Xerox had known what it had and had taken advantage of its real opportunities, it could have been 'IBM+Microsoft+Xerox.'" —Steve Jobs
body:
"If Xerox had known what it had and had taken advantage of its real opportunities, it could have been 'IBM+Microsoft+Xerox.'" —Steve Jobs

What comes to mind when you hear the name "Xerox"?

A printer brand you half remember? Or the chapter in Apple's origin story where Steve Jobs and Bill Gates took Xerox's technology to build the personal computer?

Two weeks ago, after years of poor management and under pressure from shareholders, Xerox split itself in two: one company to sell printers and copiers, the other to sell business services. It has started layoffs, and it won't rule out a sale. "The board is responsible to shareholders and will consider all offers," Xerox CEO Ursula Burns said when asked whether the company was for sale.

It is a sad story.

Consider this: the computers, laptops, and phones we use today, even the internet itself, all trace back to work first done at Xerox:

- It built a personal computer in 1973, three years before Apple;
- It invented Ethernet, the basic hardware behind broadband;
- It created the graphical user interface, before Windows and Mac OS; until then, computers showed nothing but lines of text;
- It was the first company in Silicon Valley to take up artificial intelligence research;
- Its labs gave us the laser printer;

Yet today Xerox is worth just US$9.84 billion. Apple is worth US$544.5 billion; Microsoft, US$413.5 billion.

Looking back, Xerox had a chance to match or even overtake Apple and Microsoft in the history of the personal computer. Instead, it is still just a printer company.

The irony runs deeper: Xerox was once held up as the model of a company that would bet everything on technical innovation.

## Xerox Was Built on a Technological Gamble That Paid Off

Before the copier, schools, churches, and offices relied on something called carbon paper: the blue, self-copying sheets you still come across now and then, like this:

![Carbon paper, which you can still find at small shops, banks, and on courier slips.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134820mhRKdJj5EIWtDPlM.jpg-w600)

In the 1930s, Chester Carlson, then a clerk drafting documents at a patent office, used carbon paper all the time. It was prone to mistakes, so he set out to build a machine that would do the job better.

In 1938 Carlson developed electrophotography, a way of using electricity to copy images onto carbon paper. His efforts to sell it went nowhere. After five years of funding the work himself, he finally won backing from a nonprofit, the Battelle Memorial Institute, to keep going.

Because carbon paper was already standard in every office, many companies decided there was no need for a copier. IBM, General Electric, and RCA (Radio Corporation of America) were all among those that turned Carlson down.

![Chester Carlson](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134821vy8YZs3bEjIAgl7u.jpg-w600)

In 1946 a company called Haloid took an interest. Haloid was a family business, founded in 1906 in Rochester, New York, that mainly made electrical products. Joseph Wilson, its second-generation heir, believed electrophotography was the future, so he bought Carlson's technology and hired Carlson along with it.

After the deal, Wilson renamed the process "xerography," from the root "xero," ancient Greek for "copy."

Even after eight years of work, the technology was still crude. Between 1947 and 1960 Haloid spent nearly US$75 million on xerography research, roughly twice what its regular business earned over the same period, and it had to borrow to do it. Executives put in their own savings and mortgaged their homes to keep the research going.

Thirteen years of heavy spending paid off within a single year. In 1960 Haloid launched the first automatic xerographic copier, the Xerox 914.

![The Xerox 914, a very large machine for its time](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021348211f4HxaGckjIz3swN.jpg-w600)

Xerography was far more efficient than carbon copies. Carbon paper needed a master and produced only 10 to 20 copies at a time; the new copier needed no master and had no limit on how many copies it could make. The Xerox 914 had no competitor for nearly eight years.

Xerox's sales strategy helped, too. The 914 cost US$27,000 to buy, but customers could lease one for just US$25 a month plus 4 cents a copy. Leasing let offices try Xerox's machines cheaply and then come to depend on them, and it helped Xerox place more than 20,000 copiers in short order.

![The earliest advertising poster for the Xerox 914](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134822r7Sc2YpWIOAliwU4.jpg-w600)

The 914 was so popular that Wilson renamed the whole company Xerox.

From 1960 to 1970 Xerox earned more than US$1 billion, making it the first company to earn over US$1 billion in a decade from a single technology. (The second was Apple, but that comes later.) People who bought Xerox stock early became millionaires.

More important, perhaps, the copier, or the ability to reproduce any text or image cheaply and in bulk, became the next step after printing. Copying sharply cut the cost of spreading books and other written material.

And "Xerox," like "Baidu" or "Didi" in China today, became a verb: "go Xerox it" was everyday office talk in 1960s America.

## Xerox PARC Became the Birthplace of the Personal Computer

1968 was a turning point. Carlson, the inventor of xerography, died. Then Wilson, who had big ambitions for Xerox, handed the CEO job to Peter McCollough.

Unlike Wilson, McCollough was a salesman to the core. He joined Xerox after Harvard, started selling copiers in the field, and rose to run the company's sales operations.

Before stepping aside, Wilson gave McCollough some advice. In essence: Xerox moves information with copiers, but it should do more with technology; in the coming computer age, if it wants to stay a great company, it has to handle information digitally.

McCollough took that advice.

![A high-speed typewriter IBM was promoting in 1973](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134822CEWpgj4cY6vqPyAe.jpg-w600)

In 1970, at the urging of Xerox's chief scientist, Jacob Goldman, he set up a research center in Palo Alto, California, 4,500 kilometers from headquarters: the Palo Alto Research Center, or PARC. To find Xerox its next Carlson, or its next 914, PARC hired the best researchers and engineers in America and aimed to build technology ten years ahead of anything on the market.

"Of the 100 best computer scientists in America, 76 are at PARC." That was how Bob Taylor, who ran the lab, rated his staff. As long as you were good, PARC tolerated almost anything: some people brought sleeping bags to work, some wouldn't wear shoes, and programmers with long hair and long beards were everywhere.

![PARC's beanbag meeting room](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134823Xpq4039EcCPvTY1h.jpg-w600)

PARC was also the model for today's Silicon Valley offices: no assigned desks, few rules, blackboards on every wall of every office and meeting room, and beanbags on the floor for seats.

That was radical for the time. Mainstream tech companies such as IBM were still dutifully making typewriters and punch-card machines, and their engineers wore suits to work. Nor was it only IBM: Xerox's own headquarters on the East Coast was just as old-fashioned.

This is where the world's first personal computer was born. Called the Alto, it was about the size of a trunk, had a screen, and was built for one person; whatever you typed appeared on the screen within milliseconds.

![A prototype of the Alto computer](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134823ZbhuyTWsiMeD92HV.jpg-w600)

In 1973 a personal computer like the Alto was unheard of. While PARC was building a machine a decade ahead of its time, Bill Gates was a college freshman and Steve Jobs was studying Buddhism in India.

Most computers then were the size of two or three refrigerators, wired up to special-purpose hardware and cables, and built to be shared by many users.

Computing power was scarce, so computers worked like airliners: you carried 300 passengers to split the cost, and giving a machine to one person was an absurd luxury. The memory needed for a single user alone cost US$1 million, the equivalent of chartering a whole plane for one passenger. Nor did computers have screens. People communicated with them through punch cards or typewriters, and a simple question and answer could take days.

"The architecture of computing back then was like the front line of a religious war," John Ellenby recalled, "and Xerox brought that war to a head."

Beyond the Alto's hardware, PARC's engineers worked out what should run on it. They began writing text-editing and image-processing software, and they built a graphical user interface (GUI) so that people would not have to control the computer through a command line, the way geeks did. The personal computer looks the way it does today because of mouse-driven systems like Windows.

![Left: the command-line DOS interface. Right: the graphical Windows 3.2 interface. Which would you rather use?](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134823DSkYZvyR2KIxPbh4.gif-w600Gif)

On the hardware side, there was a keyboard for typing and a mouse you could slide, point, and click. There was also a local network linking computers together, called Ethernet.

Building on all this, PARC engineer Alan Kay began work on a smaller, portable computer, the Notetaker: in effect, the ancestor of today's laptop.

With all this in place, Xerox's copiers and laser printers would have a role in the personal office. Receive mail over Ethernet, work on text and images on screen, then print them out: that was what PARC's engineers were counting on.

Seen from today, PARC's computer scientists drew up the blueprint for everyday digital life 20 years early.

Unfortunately, what Xerox cared about back then was still the printer.

## Why Did Xerox Stay a Printer Company While Apple, Microsoft, and the Internet Changed Our Lives?

Jobs's 1979 visit adds drama to the Xerox story, but it was only the spark, not the reason Xerox failed to make the personal computer.

Even before Jobs showed up, Xerox was losing its grip on its core copier business.

![PARC's working environment](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134824dlu09Bjpo2yrnt7O.jpg-w600)

After so long without competitors, Xerox did most of the damage itself. In the 1970s its wealth and its arrogance both peaked. The Xerox 914 was hugely popular and protected by patents, so profits kept rising. Managers could post good numbers without much skill, salespeople barely had to try, and life was comfortable for everyone.

With no direct competitor, Xerox also kept its complicated leasing model. The per-copy pricing was so convoluted that the first three copies might cost one rate and the 200th another. By the early 1970s, leasing a Xerox copier was a headache: thousands of pricing schemes were waiting for you.

Meanwhile, cheaper Japanese products of decent quality were flooding America in the 1970s: cars, steel, chips, and copiers too. Complacent Xerox became the top target for Japanese companies to study and improve on, and at home IBM and Kodak joined the fight. From 1971 to 1978 only 77 copier models were sold in the US; in the two-plus years from 1978 to 1980, 70 new models came onto the market.

![A group photo of PARC engineers. In the center of the top row, and second from right in the second row, are Adobe's two founders, Charles Geschke and John Warnock.](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134824d5NIGyT1uZUo8M0g.jpg-w600)

Beyond PARC, McCollough spent heavily on buying computer companies and developing technology, and several of those bets went wrong.

The purchase of computer maker SDS saddled Xerox with a loss of US$84.4 million. The "Moses" printer project, into which it had put US$90 million, was about to go into production when Xerox discovered that Kodak's rival machine was better and cheaper, and the project was scrapped.

The failures deepened the feud inside Xerox. PARC's engineers in the West saw the East Coast headquarters, which made and sold copiers, as shortsighted relics. The people at headquarters, for their part, could not make sense of PARC's technology, which was too far ahead to use in Xerox products right away.

By 1977 the second- and third-generation versions of the Alto were ready for production. But Xerox, focused on short-term profit, chose to fund a new "high-speed printer" instead and cut the money for producing the third-generation Alto. The Alto project died.

"Whether in sales, design, manufacturing, or decision-making, we are going downhill, we are not prepared for it, and what we urgently need is to reform the company," Peter Crouch, then a Xerox executive, said in 1977.

Xerox's reform ended up as a plan to invest in computer companies. Apple, which had become a hit with the Apple II, was the top pick of Xerox's executives. When they heard that Jobs wanted to tour PARC, and that he would let Xerox buy some Apple shares at a slight discount, they agreed to let him in.

![Steve Jobs at the launch of the Apple II](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702134825wpeNov7nrYVQ5M2K.jpg-w600)

As Xerox saw it, since it wasn't going to make personal computers anyway, there was no harm in letting Jobs look around.

In 1979 Xerox showed the Apple team its most closely guarded projects. Apple's engineers, who had long looked up to PARC's researchers for their skill and ideas, went home with the whole package: the graphical user interface and keyboard-and-mouse input. Later, Bill Gates also built on Xerox's technology to release Windows, a graphical operating system for personal computers.

Years later, when Jobs [recalled](http://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2011/05/16/creation-myth) the visit, he felt sorry for Xerox.

"If Xerox had known what it had and had taken advantage of its real opportunities, it could have been 'IBM+Microsoft+Xerox' combined: the largest high-technology company in the world."

But Xerox was never again the hero of the story that followed.

- In 1983, Apple released the Lisa personal computer, with a graphical interface;
- In 1985, Microsoft released the first version of Windows, also with a graphical interface. Windows went on to run 90% of the world's personal computers;
- In 2007, Apple released its first smartphone, the iPhone; in 2011, Apple became the world's most valuable company;
- In 2015, the number of people online worldwide reached 3.3 billion.
